title: Crystals
objective: After this level you can explain how crystals form.
summary: A crystal's particles repeat a pattern in every direction: salt grains are cubes, snowflakes six-fold. Crystals grow from solutions, melts or vapor; slow growth makes giants like Naica's.

cards.headline: In 2000, miners in Mexico broke into a cave of crystals up to 11 meters long.
cards.body: How does anything grow that big? Start with what makes a crystal a crystal.

cards.fact: A crystal is a solid whose particles sit in a pattern that repeats in every direction.
cards.context: And the outside often shows the inside. Level 43's salt grid is cubic, so salt crystals are cubes. In ice, water molecules line up in a hexagonal pattern, which is why every snowflake has six-fold symmetry. Look closely at a snowflake and you're seeing the arrangement of its molecules, made big enough to catch on your sleeve.

cards.headline: Joining the pattern
cards.body: Crystals grow as particles join the pattern, each atom, ion or molecule settling into its place. They can grow from a solution, from a cooling melt, or straight from a vapor. You've met that last one already: Level 10's frost, water vapor turning straight into ice on a cold window, is crystals growing from a gas.

cards.headline: Slow and steady grows giants
cards.body: Speed matters. Crystals that form fast stay small; slow growth makes bigger ones. Naica's gypsum crystals grew in hot, mineral-rich water that stayed in a narrow, steady temperature range for many hundreds of thousands of years. With that much time, a crystal can grow to 11 meters. Patience, on a geological scale.

mascot.line: I once got impatient waiting for toast. Naica has me rethinking my life.

cards.headline: Crystals: grown
learned: A crystal's particles repeat a pattern in every direction
Salt grains are cubes; snowflakes are six-fold
Crystals grow from solutions, melts or vapor
Slow growth makes big crystals, like Naica's giants

questions.prompt: What makes a solid a crystal?

options.label: It is clear and sparkly
options.rationale: Looks aren't the test; the inner pattern is.

options.label: It is made of only one kind of atom
options.rationale: Salt is a crystal of two kinds of ion.

options.label: It formed deep underground
options.rationale: Frost and snowflakes are crystals formed in the air.

options.label: Its particles repeat a pattern in every direction

questions.explanation: In a crystal, the atoms, ions or molecules sit in a pattern that repeats in all directions.

questions.prompt: Why did the gypsum crystals in Mexico's Naica cave grow so large?

options.label: They formed in one sudden flash of hot lava
options.rationale: Fast cooling makes small crystals, not giants.

options.label: They grew slowly in water at a steady temperature
Miners fed extra minerals into the water
options.rationale: The crystals were already there when miners arrived in 2000.

options.label: Cave air makes every crystal grow huge
options.rationale: It was slow growth in warm water, not the air.

questions.explanation: Naica's crystals grew for many hundreds of thousands of years in mineral-rich water held in a narrow temperature range. Slow growth makes big crystals.

questions.prompt: Level 10 described frost forming on a cold window. As crystal growth, where does frost come from?

options.label: Liquid dew that slowly melts
options.rationale: Frost skips the liquid stage entirely.

options.label: Water vapor turning straight into ice
Molten rock that cools down
options.rationale: That's growth from a melt, not frost.

questions.explanation: Frost is deposition: water vapor joining an ice crystal pattern directly, crystal growth from a gas.
